01-build-story.md.title: We built an AI that isn't allowed to make anything up, then pointed it at India's coal plant approvals
01-build-story.md.description: On page 18 of a 246-page government filing, a 1,320 MW coal expansion on the Hasdeo River skipped its public hearing. Vakeel is an AI on AWS that reads India's environmental clearance filings for the people next door, proves every number against the page, and helps them object.
01-build-story.md.body:
*Environmental Hacks 2026 · Bharat Builds Tour · Air track*

On 20 June 2025, a government committee in New Delhi met to decide the future of six coal power plants. Its minutes are public on PARIVESH, the national clearance portal: **246 pages, 620,940 characters**.

On page 18 there's this line:

> "Public hearing for the 2x660 MW (Phase - II) is exempted as per S.O. 1247(E)…"

That's a 1,320 MW coal expansion at Korba, Chhattisgarh, 2.2 km from the Barpall reserved forest. It draws 104,110 cubic metres a day from the Hasdeo River, the river at the heart of Hasdeo Arand, where Adivasi communities have fought coal mining for over a decade. On page 25, the committee **recommended it**.

S.O. 1247(E) is a March 2021 amendment to India's EIA Notification. When a project's clearance lapses before it's finished, the committee may waive the public hearing if the project is already **at least half built**. Korba was more than 75% built. The people who will breathe its smoke never got a hearing.

## Why this is an air problem, not a paperwork problem

- Studies link pollution from India's coal power plants to **as many as 115,000 premature deaths a year**.
- In **July 2025**, a revised notification exempted **78% of India's coal plants** from installing flue-gas desulphurisation (sulphur scrubbers).
- Committee scrutiny is thin. One analysis found the river-valley committee **rejected nothing** in six years.

That leaves the environmental clearance as the last point where anyone can say no to more coal smoke, more river water drawn and more forest lost. The law gives the people next door a voice there, through public hearings and written objections. But you can't object to a document you can't read.

So we built **Vakeel** (Hindi for *advocate*): an AI that reads these filings for the people next door, and helps them object before approval.

![Vakeel project page: the Korba expansion decoded, every figure linked to its source page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/adhavan18/vakeel/main/assets/screenshots/04-project.png)

## The hard part wasn't reading. It was trust.

An LLM summarising legal documents is easy to build and dangerous to ship. If it invents one number ("the plant will displace 2,000 families") in a letter a citizen signs and sends to a government committee, the whole idea collapses. So we designed Vakeel around one rule: **the AI is not allowed to say anything it can't prove from the page.**

1. **Tool-forced structured output.** Amazon Bedrock (Nova 2 Lite) is called through the Converse API with a single tool whose input schema is the shape we want: facts, nearby places, concerns, the committee's decision. Each item must include a **verbatim quote** and a **page number**.
2. **A deterministic verifier.** Code normalises the quote and searches the actual PDF text for it. It also checks that the claimed number appears *inside* the quote. No match, no claim. On this filing alone, the verifier threw out 26 claims; across our three real filings it has kept 219 and rejected 65. They're shown in a section called *What Vakeel refused to tell you*.
3. **Tables fight back.** PDF extraction scrambles tables, so a true fact like "Barpall R.F. · 2.2 km" can fail an exact-quote match. Rather than loosen the rule, we added a second deterministic check: the name and the number must sit together in one row of a real page, and that row's actual text becomes the quote.
4. **The model never does the math.** "₹4,887 crore of climate damage a year" is computed in Python from the plant's stated capacity × plant load factor (CEA) × emission rate × India's social cost of carbon (Ricke et al., *Nature Climate Change*, 2018). Every factor and its source is one click away in the UI.
5. **Headlines can't sneak in numbers either.** A second Bedrock pass writes the plain-language headline and the Hindi/Odia translations. Any number in them that isn't in the verified data gets the text thrown away and replaced.
6. **Never overstate a decision.** The model once called an approved *Terms of Reference* (permission to *study* a plant) "recommended for clearance". A small rule now makes sure that can never be shown.

## Parallel agents with Step Functions

Committee minutes bundle several projects, and describe each one twice: once with its details near the front, again with the committee's deliberations near the back. Vakeel's segmenter stitches each project's two halves back together. Then a **Step Functions Map state** fans out one Bedrock agent per project, three at a time, with retries. Every agent streams progress into DynamoDB, and the UI shows six lanes reading in parallel. The whole 246-page filing goes from queued to finished in 52 seconds, for roughly 200k tokens.

![Six Bedrock agents reading one filing in parallel, with a live log](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/adhavan18/vakeel/main/assets/screenshots/02-agents.png)

## A human must sign. Step Functions waits.

Vakeel drafts a formal objection to the committee. The grounds are built **by code** from verified concerns, each with its quote and page. Bedrock writes only the opening and the requests, and those are rejected if they contain any number at all.

Then the objection state machine reaches a `lambda:invoke.waitForTaskToken` state and stops. Nothing happens until a real person reads the letter and types an exact sentence ("I object to proposal IA/CG/THE/532429/2025"). The API checks the phrase *and* that the SHA-256 of the letter they read matches the letter on record. Only then does it call `SendTaskSuccess`. The signed letter gets a receipt hash, and the citizen sends it from their own email so it carries their legal identity.

## What fought back

- **"Explicit deny in a service control policy."** Our new AWS account is a *project* pinned to a home region (Sydney). Deploying to us-east-1 failed on Lambda, DynamoDB and S3, even with AdministratorAccess. The fix was in Settings → Projects → Additional info: deploy to `ap-southeast-2`. Bedrock's `global.` inference profile made Nova 2 Lite work from Sydney with no code changes.
- **Contaminated sections.** Our first segmenter gave the last project 136 pages, including the other projects' annexures, so NTPC's Odisha plant "acquired" a river from Chhattisgarh. Splitting on both kinds of agenda headings fixed it.
- **Cost on a $100 account.** We built in an atomic daily Bedrock call cap in DynamoDB, one Step Functions execution per document (execution name = document id), SHA-256 dedupe so no PDF is paid for twice, and API throttling.

## Stack

Amazon Bedrock (Nova 2 Lite) · AWS Step Functions · AWS Lambda · Amazon DynamoDB · Amazon S3 · Amazon CloudFront · Amazon API Gateway · Amazon Location Service · Amazon Polly (the launch video's voice) · CloudFormation. Frontend: React, Tailwind, Leaflet.

## What's next

Watching PARIVESH for new filings by district, then WhatsApp and voice alerts in local languages, so a farmer near the next proposed plant hears about it from Vakeel before the objection window closes, not after.

## Sources

- S.O. 1247(E), 18 March 2021, amendment to the EIA Notification 2006 (public-hearing exemption for projects at least 50% implemented): https://dste.py.gov.in/SEIAA/pdf/Notifications/N38.pdf
- Coal power and premature deaths in India: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/coal-fired-power-in-india-may-cause-more-than-100000-premature-deaths-annually/
- July 2025 FGD exemption for 78% of coal plants (CREA via Down To Earth): https://www.downtoearth.org.in/energy/most-sulphur-dioxide-around-delhi-comes-from-coal-plants-exempted-from-pollution-rules-crea
- EAC rejection analysis (SANDRP): https://sandrp.in/2013/02/05/analysis-of-moefs-eac-on-river-valley-projects-the-expert-approval-committee-has-zero-rejection-in-six-years/
- Hasdeo Arand protests: https://scroll.in/article/1031123/threatened-by-coal-mining-hasdeo-arand-forest-is-receiving-a-groundswell-of-support-on-the-internet
- Source filing (EAC Thermal minutes, 20 June 2025): https://parivesh.nic.in/utildoc/131396604_1751547453000.pdf
- Live app: https://d4i9n8m04ddaa.cloudfront.net · Code: https://github.com/adhavan18/vakeel

02-verifier.md.title: How we fact-check an LLM against a 246-page government PDF
02-verifier.md.description: Five deterministic rules that stop an LLM from putting a made-up number into a legal objection: verbatim quotes, page checks, table-row matching, a number guard on generated prose, and showing what was thrown away.
02-verifier.md.body:
*Part 2 of the Vakeel build log · Environmental Hacks 2026 · #BharatBuilds*

Vakeel reads India's environmental clearance filings (Expert Appraisal Committee minutes, EIA reports) and turns them into plain-language warnings for the people who live next to coal plants and mines. Those warnings end up in **signed legal objections**, so a hallucinated number isn't a quality issue. It's the citizen's credibility on the line.

This post is about the piece of code that makes that safe: a verifier that checks every AI claim against the source PDF before anyone sees it.

## Rule 1: no quote, no claim

We call Amazon Bedrock (Nova 2 Lite) through the Converse API with **one tool** and `toolChoice` forced to it. The tool's input schema *is* the output we want, so the model can only answer by filling it:

```json
{ "key": "water_m3_per_day", "value": 104110,
  "label": "Fresh water drawn per day",
  "quote": "The water requirement for the proposed project is estimated as 104110 m3/day",
  "page": 14 }
```

Every fact, nearby river or forest, concern, and committee decision must carry a `quote` copied character-for-character and the `page` it came from.

## Rule 2: the quote must exist, and the number must be inside it

PDF text is messy: words split across lines (`com\npleted`), odd spaces (`m 3/day`), stray glyphs. So both the quote and every page get the same normalisation (lowercase, keep only `[a-z0-9]`), and we search:

```python
def norm(text):
    return re.sub(r"[^0-9a-z]", "", text.lower())

page = index.locate(item["quote"])          # None if not on any page
if number_digits(item["value"]) not in norm(item["quote"]):
    reject("value does not appear in its quote")
```

The second check catches a subtle failure: the model quotes a real sentence but reports a *different* number, or quietly converts units ("32.93 LMT" becomes 3,293,000 tonnes). We ask for the number exactly as written and do unit conversion in code, where it can be tested.

## Rule 3: tables need their own check

On our first real run the verifier rejected *"Barpall R.F., 2.2 km"* and *"Hasdeo River, 2.4 km"*. Both are true. The problem: they sit in a table, and PDF extraction turns a table row into `1 Barpall R. \nF.\n2.2 SW`, so a "verbatim" quote never matches.

We didn't loosen the rule; we added a second deterministic test for places. The **name** and the **distance** must appear together in one row of the same page (within 60 normalised characters), and the actual row text from the PDF becomes the quote:

```python
row = index.find_row("Barpall R. F.", 2.2)   # -> (13, "Barpall R. F. 2.2")
```

A made-up forest with a made-up distance still fails.

## Rule 4: generated prose can't introduce numbers

A second Bedrock pass writes the headline a villager will read, plus Hindi and Odia translations. Prose is where hallucinations hide, so we pull every number out of the headline and check it against the set of verified values. If one doesn't match, the headline is replaced with a deterministic template. We also block single-digit numbers that are followed by a unit ("schools within 5 km"), because that's exactly how an unsupported claim slipped through in testing.

## Rule 5: show what was thrown away

Rejected claims aren't silently dropped. Each project page has a section called **"What Vakeel refused to tell you"**, listing every claim the AI made that couldn't be proven, and why. On our first filing, that was 26 claims; across three filings, 65 rejected and 219 kept. Judges, journalists and lawyers can see the system's honesty for themselves instead of taking our word for it.

![What Vakeel refused to tell you](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/adhavan18/vakeel/main/assets/screenshots/06-refused.png)

## What this bought us

- Every number on screen has a green **✓ p.14** tick that opens the exact page with the quote highlighted.

![The evidence drawer: the quote highlighted on the real PDF page](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/adhavan18/vakeel/main/assets/screenshots/05-evidence-drawer.png)
- The objection letter's grounds are assembled by code from verified concerns only. Bedrock writes the opening and the requests, and those are rejected if they contain *any* digit.
- Money figures (₹4,887 crore a year of climate damage for one plant) are computed in Python from sourced factors, never by the model.

An LLM is a great reader and a terrible witness. Vakeel lets it read, then makes it prove everything.

03-human-signature-step-functions.md.title: A legal signature as a Step Functions state: human-in-the-loop with waitForTaskToken
03-human-signature-step-functions.md.description: How Vakeel uses AWS Step Functions' waitForTaskToken to make a legal objection impossible to send until a real person reads it and signs, with a hash check on the exact letter they read.
03-human-signature-step-functions.md.body:
*Part 3 of the Vakeel build log · Environmental Hacks 2026 · #BharatBuilds*

Vakeel helps residents object to coal plants and mines before they're cleared. It drafts a formal objection to India's Expert Appraisal Committee from the committee's own record. The one thing it must **never** do is send a legal document in someone's name on its own.

Here's how we made "a human must read and sign this first" a hard property of the system rather than a promise in a prompt.

![A filing decoded: committee decisions per project, on a map](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/adhavan18/vakeel/main/assets/screenshots/03-filing-map.png)

## The state machine

```
Draft ──► AwaitSignature ──► File
  │       (waitForTaskToken,      │
  │        7-day timeout)         │
  └────────── Expire ◄────────────┘   (any failure or timeout)
```

```yaml
AwaitSignature:
  Type: Task
  Resource: arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke.waitForTaskToken
  Parameters:
    FunctionName: !Ref AwaitSignatureFunction
    Payload:
      objectionId.$: $.objectionId
      taskToken.$: $$.Task.Token
  TimeoutSeconds: 604800
  Catch: [{ ErrorEquals: [States.ALL], Next: Expire }]
  Next: File
```

The `AwaitSignature` Lambda does one thing: it stores the task token on the objection record in DynamoDB and returns. The execution then **pauses for up to seven days**, costing nothing. If nobody signs, it times out into `Expire` and nothing is filed.

## Two checks before SendTaskSuccess

The signing endpoint is the only place that can resume the workflow, and it checks two independent things:

```python
if normalise(body["phrase"]) != normalise(obj["phrase"]):
    raise HttpError(400, f"Type exactly: {obj['phrase']}")
if body["letterHash"] != obj["letterHash"]:
    raise HttpError(409, "The letter changed since you read it.")
sfn.send_task_success(taskToken=obj["taskToken"], output='{"signed": true}')
```

1. **An exact phrase**, e.g. `I object to proposal IA/CG/THE/532429/2025`. Typing the proposal number is deliberate friction: you can't sign by accident, and you know which project you're objecting to.
2. **The SHA-256 of the letter the citizen actually read.** The browser sends back the hash it displayed. If the stored letter changed in any way between reading and signing, the signature is refused.

Only then does `File` run. It writes a receipt, `sha256(letterHash | name | signedAt)`, and increments the public counters.

## Why the model can't put words in the citizen's mouth

The letter is built mostly by code:
- **Grounds of objection** come from verified concerns. Each one quotes the committee's record with a page number, and every quote has already passed the verifier.
- **Climate figures** are computed in Python and labelled as estimates.
- **Bedrock writes only the opening paragraph and the requests**, and the drafting code throws those away if they contain any digit at all. A model can't invent a statistic it isn't allowed to write.

## Why not just a database flag?

We could have stored `status = awaiting_signature` and polled. Step Functions gave us more for less code:
- the pause, the timeout and the expiry path are declared, not hand-written;
- every objection has an execution history showing exactly when it was drafted, signed and filed, which is an audit trail for a legal document;
- execution names are unique (`obj-<id>`), so a double-click can't start two workflows.

The same pattern secured last round's winners (Beacon's voice-approved remediation, Suraksha's consent gates). For a civic tool it fits even better: the human isn't approving a deployment, they're putting their name to a legal objection.

04-region-scp-fix.md.title: "Explicit deny in a service control policy": deploying on the new AWS project accounts (and why AdministratorAccess didn't help)
04-region-scp-fix.md.description: New AWS project accounts for the hackathon can fail with 'explicit deny in a service control policy' even with AdministratorAccess. Here's why, and the two-minute fix.
04-region-scp-fix.md.body:
*A practical fix for Environmental Hacks participants · #BharatBuilds*

If you made a fresh AWS account for the hackathon and everything except a few services fails with

```
User: arn:aws:iam::<account>:user/<you> is not authorized to perform: lambda:ListFunctions
... with an explicit deny in a service control policy:
arn:aws:organizations::<org>:policy/o-xxxx/service_control_policy/p-xxxx
```

this is for you. We lost about an hour to it while building Vakeel. Here's what's going on and the two-minute fix.

## Symptoms

- Bedrock, CloudFront, IAM and STS work.
- Lambda, DynamoDB, Step Functions, CloudFormation, API Gateway, S3 `CreateBucket`, Polly, Lightsail creates and more all return **explicit deny in a service control policy**.
- Attaching `AdministratorAccess` to your IAM user changes nothing.
- Upgrading from the Free plan to Paid changes nothing.

## Why

New accounts created through the new sign-in experience (AWS Builder ID → **settings.aws.com** with *Projects / Team / Billing / Support*) are **projects** inside an AWS-managed organization. The org applies a service control policy, and an SCP sits *above* IAM: an explicit deny there can't be overridden by any IAM policy, including admin.

The SCP pins the project to a **home region**. Global services (IAM, CloudFront, STS) pass. Most of the AWS CLI's default region, `us-east-1`, does not.

## The fix

1. Open **settings.aws.com → Projects → your project → Additional info**.
2. Read the **Region** field. Ours was *Asia Pacific (Sydney) ap-southeast-2*.
3. Deploy there:

```bash
aws configure set region ap-southeast-2
aws lambda list-functions --max-items 1   # works now
```

Everything we needed worked in the home region: Lambda, Step Functions, DynamoDB, CloudFormation, API Gateway, S3, Polly, Location Service and Textract.

## Two gotchas after you switch regions

**Bedrock model IDs.** Not every model ID is available everywhere. From Sydney, these worked for us:

```
global.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0     ✅  (global cross-region inference profile)
apac.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0          ✅
apac.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0       ❌  invalid identifier
amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0            ❌  on-demand not supported, use an inference profile
```

**S3 presigned uploads from the browser.** If you presign against the global endpoint, a brand-new bucket outside us-east-1 answers with **307 Temporary Redirect**, and browsers refuse redirects on CORS uploads. Pin the client to the regional endpoint:

```python
s3 = boto3.client(
    "s3",
    region_name="ap-southeast-2",
    endpoint_url="https://s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com",
    config=Config(signature_version="s3v4", s3={"addressing_style": "virtual"}),
)
```

**Bonus (Windows + AWS CLI v1):** `aws cloudformation package` doesn't resolve SAM `Globals: Function: CodeUri`, so every function gets a zip of your template folder and fails with `No module named 'handlers'`. Put `CodeUri` on each function, and build the zip yourself with forward-slash paths.

## While you're in Settings

The upgrade flow lets you set a **monthly spend limit** (we used $20) that pauses the project if it's reached, plus alerts at 50/75/90%. That's a better guardrail than a budget email when you're learning on real infrastructure. Skip the "pause idle resources" option if your demo needs to be up while judges look at it.

Good luck. If this saved you an hour, go build something that matters with it.

— Team behind **Vakeel**, an AI that reads India's environmental clearance filings for the people who live next to them.

05-cost-guardrails.md.title: Running parallel Bedrock agents on a $100 AWS account without waking up to a bill
05-cost-guardrails.md.description: Seven guardrails that let a public upload button drive parallel Amazon Bedrock agents on a $100 AWS account: an atomic daily cap in DynamoDB, idempotent executions, hash dedupe and more.
05-cost-guardrails.md.body:
*Part 4 of the Vakeel build log · Environmental Hacks 2026 · #BharatBuilds*

Vakeel reads 250-page Indian government filings with a fleet of Amazon Bedrock agents, one per project, orchestrated by AWS Step Functions. It's public: anyone can upload a PDF. It also runs on a brand-new hackathon account with $100 of credits and a $20 monthly spend limit.

That combination is how people end up with surprise bills: a public upload button wired to an LLM, fanned out in parallel, with retries. Here are the guardrails we built so it can't run away. Each one is a few lines of code.

## 1. A daily Bedrock cap that can't race

Every Bedrock call first takes a ticket from one DynamoDB item per day. The increment and the limit check are a single conditional write, so twenty parallel Lambdas can't all read "59" and all go ahead:

```python
def budget_ok() -> bool:
    day = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    try:
        table.update_item(
            Key={"pk": "BUDGET", "sk": day},
            UpdateExpression="ADD calls :one SET #ttl = :ttl",
            ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(calls) OR calls < :max",
            ExpressionAttributeNames={"#ttl": "ttl"},
            ExpressionAttributeValues={":one": 1, ":max": MAX_CALLS, ":ttl": int(time.time()) + 7 * 86400},
        )
        return True
    except ClientError as exc:
        if exc.response["Error"]["Code"] == "ConditionalCheckFailedException":
            return False
        raise
```

When the cap is hit, the call raises `BudgetExceeded("Daily Bedrock call budget reached; try again tomorrow.")` and the run stops. It fails closed. The cap is a CloudFormation parameter (`MaxBedrockCallsPerDay`), so we lowered it from 150 to 60 during judging week without a code change. The TTL cleans up old counters for free.

## 2. Pay for a document once, ever

Two layers, both deterministic:

- **The Step Functions execution name is the document id.** `start_execution(name=f"doc-{doc_id}")` throws `ExecutionAlreadyExists` on a second attempt, so a double-click, a retry or a replayed request can't start a second paid run. We catch that one error and carry on.
- **SHA-256 of the file bytes.** Before any model sees the PDF, the first state hashes it and looks up `HASH#<digest>`. If someone uploads a filing Vakeel has already read, it links to the existing analysis and logs: *"Vakeel has already read this exact document. Opening the existing analysis instead of paying to read it twice."*

## 3. Bound the input before it reaches the model

All limits live in one config file, not scattered through handlers:

```python
MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES = 25 * 1024 * 1024   # checked on request, then on the real S3 object before analysis
MAX_PAGES = 400
MAX_PROJECTS_PER_DOC = 8
SEGMENT_HEAD_CHARS = 60_000           # per-project context, front half
SEGMENT_TAIL_CHARS = 45_000           # committee deliberations, back half
```

The biggest saving wasn't a limit, though. It was **not sending the whole document**. Committee minutes describe each project twice, once near the front and once in the deliberations near the back. Vakeel's segmenter stitches each project's two halves together, so each agent reads its own project, not 620,940 characters of everyone else's. A 246-page filing costs roughly 200k input tokens in total.

## 4. Parallel, but polite

The Step Functions Map state runs **three agents at a time** (`MaxConcurrency: 3`), not "as many as there are projects". Bedrock throttling is retried with backoff in the state machine itself, so a Lambda never sits in a sleep loop on the meter:

```yaml
Retry:
  - ErrorEquals: [ThrottlingException, ServiceUnavailableException, Lambda.TooManyRequestsException]
    IntervalSeconds: 5
    BackoffRate: 2
    MaxAttempts: 3
```

The public HTTP API is throttled at 10 requests a second with a burst of 20, which is plenty for people and useless for a script.

## 5. Small model, forced structure

Extraction runs on **Amazon Nova 2 Lite** through the `global.` cross-region inference profile, called with Converse and a single forced tool (`toolChoice`). The model can only answer by filling our JSON schema, so there's no chatty preamble to pay for and no retry-until-it-parses loop. All the arithmetic (CO₂, the climate-cost estimate, water in people-per-day) happens in Python afterwards, which also means it costs nothing.

## 6. Serverless all the way down

Lambda (Python 3.12 on arm64), Step Functions, DynamoDB on-demand, S3 and CloudFront. With no traffic, the bill is effectively zero; there's no idle cluster or database instance to forget about.

## What it actually cost

Three real filings (732 pages, 17 projects), dozens of development runs and the live demo: **well under a dollar of actual spend** when AWS's budget alert arrived.

The alert itself was alarming: a *forecast* of several hundred dollars for the month. That's an extrapolation from a few busy development days, not money spent. Check *actual* versus *forecast* before you panic, and keep a spend limit on the account anyway. Ours is the backstop behind every guardrail above.

## The checklist

1. One atomic daily counter in front of every model call, failing closed.
2. Execution name = idempotency key.
3. Hash the input; never pay twice for the same bytes.
4. Bounded inputs in one config file, and send each agent only what it needs.
5. Concurrency limits and backoff in the orchestrator, not in your code.
6. Forced tool output on a small model; do the math in code.
7. Serverless, so idle costs nothing.

Live: https://d4i9n8m04ddaa.cloudfront.net · Code: https://github.com/adhavan18/vakeel

06-launch-film-in-code.md.title: We made our launch film in code: Amazon Polly, React and a synthesizer written in numpy
06-launch-film-in-code.md.description: How we built a beat-synced hackathon launch film entirely in code: Amazon Polly narration, React scenes with Remotion, a numpy synthesizer and PyAV encoding.
06-launch-film-in-code.md.body:
*Part 5 of the Vakeel build log · Environmental Hacks 2026 · #BharatBuilds*

**▶ The film:** <YOUTUBE LINK>

Our hackathon project, Vakeel, reads India's coal plant approvals for the people who live next door. We had a working product on AWS and about a day for the demo video. Screen recordings stuttered, our editing software couldn't keep up, and `ffmpeg.exe` was blocked on the build machine by Windows application control.

So we built the film the way we build software: as code that renders, with every number pulled from the live product and every cut computed. Here's the pipeline.

## 1. Narration with Amazon Polly

The script is a JSON file with one line of narration per scene. A 50-line Python script sends each line to Amazon Polly's generative engine (voice **Kajal**, `en-IN`) and writes one WAV per scene plus a manifest of exact durations:

```python
audio = polly.synthesize_speech(
    Text=scene["vo"], VoiceId="Kajal", Engine="generative",
    LanguageCode="en-IN", OutputFormat="pcm", SampleRate="16000",
)["AudioStream"].read()
manifest[scene["id"]] = round(len(audio) / 2 / 16000, 2)
```

Those durations drive everything else. Change a line, re-run Polly, and the whole film re-times itself. The Polly takes also became the **pacing guide** for the founder's own voice: a small browser recorder shows each line as a teleprompter, plays the Polly version, and saves takes straight into the project.

## 2. Scenes in React with Remotion

Each scene is a React component rendered frame by frame by [Remotion](https://www.remotion.dev). Product footage isn't a screen recording. A Playwright script captures **2× screenshots** of every state of the live app, along with the on-screen position of every button the cursor will click. The film then animates a virtual camera (keyframed zoom and pan), a cursor that glides and clicks, and crossfades between states. The result is Screen Studio-style footage with no dropped frames, because there are no frames to drop.

The kinetic type is timed to the narration from its own text. We estimate when a phrase is spoken from its character position in the line, with extra weight for pauses at commas and full stops:

```js
const weight = (s) => [...s].reduce((a, c) => a + (".?!".includes(c) ? 7 : c === "," ? 4 : 1), 0);
const at = (scene, phrase) =>
  VO_DELAY + (weight(scene.vo.slice(0, scene.vo.indexOf(phrase))) / weight(scene.vo)) * scene.voSeconds * FPS;
```

It's crude and it works: "246 pages" slams onto the screen as the voice says it, with whichever voice is recorded.

## 3. A beat-locked score, synthesized in numpy

We wanted cuts on the beat, so we picked a tempo where a beat is a whole number of frames: **14 frames at 30 fps = 128.57 BPM**. Every scene is a whole number of bars, long enough for its narration:

```js
const frames = Math.max(scene.bars, Math.ceil((VO_DELAY + vo * FPS + TAIL) / BAR)) * BAR;
```

A Python script computes the same timeline and writes the music to match: kick, clap, hats, sub bass, detuned-saw stabs and arpeggios, all built from sine waves and noise in numpy and sidechained to the kick. Each scene has an energy level: tense intro, a drop on the logo, a full groove for the product, a quiet breakdown for the human cost. Risers lead into the drops, and every on-screen "slam" gets a hit at the same frame the text lands, because both sides use the same timing function.

## 4. Mixing and encoding without ffmpeg.exe

Remotion renders a JPEG sequence. Then a Python script:

- mixes the narration over the score, **ducking the music** under every line with short ramps (the same curve as the in-browser preview);
- encodes H.264 and AAC through **PyAV**, which bundles its own libx264, so the blocked binary never runs;
- writes an `.srt` caption file timed from the narration.

A mistake worth sharing: our first mix had the voice at 0 dB over the music in the busy sections. It sounded fine on laptop speakers and would have been mush on a phone. We measured voice-to-music level per scene, then raised the voice 3.5 dB and ducked the music deeper, to roughly +10 dB.

## 5. The film can't drift from the product

Every number on screen came from the live API on the day we rendered: 246 pages read in 52 seconds, 219 claims verified, 65 rejected, ₹4,887 crore of estimated climate damage a year. When the product's numbers changed, we re-captured the screenshots instead of leaving stale stats on screen. When the narration changes, the music and the cuts follow.

## The stack

- **Voice:** Amazon Polly (generative, Kajal, en-IN), then the founder's own takes
- **Visuals:** Remotion (React), Playwright captures of the live app on CloudFront
- **Music:** numpy and scipy, written from scratch
- **Encode:** PyAV (libx264 + AAC)
